meta.title: Reading the Film Before You Hear It
meta.theme: what a subtitle has to leave out, and what the gap does to the person watching

format.format_verified: 2026-09: five sentences, TITA, +3 with no negative marking, consistent in released papers 2016 to 2025; re-verify against each new official paper

traps.description: The outlier keeps the subject and offers itself as the comparison a fair account might make, which is enough disguise at this tier. The decoy is the sentence listing what is cut first, whose three quick items give it a texture unlike the explanation around it.

meta.learning_objective: follow an explanation from its constraint to its effect, and notice the sentence that has stopped explaining in order to take a side

quality.adversarial_review: The rival is the sentence naming what disappears first, the hesitations and the politeness: it is a list where everything around it is explanation, so a reader eliminating by texture may take it. It stays because the shortening announced in the opening has to be given a content before the hard case can be understood as hard, and because the joke that arrives early is the extreme version of exactly that shortening. The sentence about dubbing and self-congratulation is the only one that stops explaining and starts scoring a point, and it answers a quarrel the paragraph has never mentioned.

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General account of subtitling constraints; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: An easy-tier stance break in a field where opinions are plentiful, which is the point: the paragraph is explaining a constraint, and a verdict on a rival practice has no stage in that explanation.

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: A joke built on delay is the hardest case, since the line appears while the actor is still winding up and the reader reaches the ending first.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: Dubbing spares an audience all of this, and the preference for subtitles among serious filmgoers is largely a form of self-congratulation.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: A subtitle has to fit a line the eye can take in at a glance, which means that most of what is said arrives shortened.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: The viewer therefore follows two performances slightly out of step, and grows so used to the gap that the film comes to seem as though it had been written that way.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: What goes first is whatever carries no information: the hesitations, the repetitions, the politeness that pads the space around a request.

builder.prompt: Build the four-sentence explanation of what a subtitle does to a film, from the constraint to the viewer. The sentence that has stopped explaining and started taking sides is your answer.

explanation.spine_note: The core explains one constraint and follows it to its effect. It opens with the physical limit, a line the eye can take in at once, and the shortening that follows from it, then says what is cut first. The third sentence takes the hardest case, a joke that depends on timing, and shows the shortening at its most damaging, and the fourth states what the whole arrangement does to the person watching. Constraint, what is lost, hardest case, effect.

core_roles.label: C
core_roles.why_here: It states the limit everything else follows from, and it is the only sentence that says why anything has to be cut at all.

core_roles.label: E
core_roles.why_here: 'What goes first' answers the shortening just announced and gives it a content, which the hardest case then depends on.

core_roles.label: A
core_roles.why_here: It takes the same shortening to its extreme, where the loss is not filler but timing, and so shows the constraint at full strength.

core_roles.label: D
core_roles.why_here: 'Therefore' gathers the constraint and its worst case into a statement about the viewer, which is where the explanation was heading.

links.explanation: 'What goes first' refers to the shortening the previous sentence announced, and orders the losses it creates.
The hardest case is set against the easy losses just listed, so the sentence continues the same scale rather than starting a new one.
'Therefore' draws the consequence of a reader who is always slightly ahead, which is exactly the case just described.

explanation.violation_named: The four core sentences explain how subtitling works and what it costs. The odd sentence leaves that explanation to deliver a verdict on people who prefer subtitles, and on a rival practice the paragraph has not been discussing. It is a change of stance, from an account to a judgement about taste.
explanation.why_it_breaks: Nothing in the paragraph has raised a choice between two ways of translating a film, so the comparison answers a question nobody here has asked, and the sentence that follows is concerned with a viewer's adjustment rather than with a viewer's motives. The sentence also ends the enquiry: once the preference has been explained away as vanity, there is nothing for the closing sentence to conclude about.
explanation.trap_exposed: The camouflage is that it sounds even-handed: it mentions the same films and the same audience, and it appears to offer the comparison a fair account owes. Fairness of that sort is not a tie. The decoy is the list of what disappears first, whose three quick items make it feel like an aside, though the hardest case is unintelligible without knowing what the ordinary losses are.

exclusion_analysis.label: C
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It states a technical limitation and no more, so a reader looking for the paragraph's idea may treat it as a preliminary that could be assumed.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it nothing explains why anything is shortened, and the losses, the joke and the viewer's adjustment all follow from a constraint the paragraph never states.

exclusion_analysis.label: E
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It is a list of three items in a set of ordinary sentences, and lists always look like illustration that could be spared.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the shortening has no content, and the hardest case is hard by comparison with nothing.

exclusion_analysis.label: A
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It is the only sentence about comedy, and a reader may take it for a specialised aside rather than a stage of the explanation.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the paragraph never shows the loss doing real damage, and the two performances out of step in the last sentence have no case behind them.

exclusion_analysis.label: D
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It concludes with a claim about habit and illusion that goes beyond anything the earlier sentences measured, so it can look like a different essay's ending.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the explanation lists costs and never says what the costs come to for the person watching, which is the point the sequence was building.

explanation.detection_habit: Ask whether the paragraph is explaining or arguing about taste. A sentence that ranks two practices, or the people who prefer them, needs a dispute to belong to, and an explanation is not a dispute.

mentor.challenge: Five sentences about words on the bottom of a screen. Four of them work out what the constraint does, and one tells you what to think of people who like it.
mentor.takeaway: The moment a sentence starts settling a preference, check whether the paragraph ever opened one.
